newsitem.title: USA: NYC Auth takes Lockheed contract off board agenda.
newsitem.headline: NYC Auth takes Lockheed contract off board agenda.

text.p: The New York State Metropolitan Transportation Wednesday said it granted a request by New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani to delay acting on a $95 million contract for Lockheed Martin Corp.

"Based on a request from Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, I have asked MTA New York City Transit to delay for one month action on a contract with Lockheed Martin Corporation for outsourcing information and technology services," said Mark Shaw, executive director of the MTA, in prepared remarks.
The board of the MTA was scheduled to vote on the contract on Thursday.
Giuliani, in a letter to Virgil Conway, the chairman of the MTA, said the proposed contract would have a major impact on New York City, and noted the city had decided not to business with the firm.
Saying he had asked the New York City Commissioner of Investigation to review the matter, he added: "There is no reason to rush this decision without proper deliberation."
The New York Observer, in its May 26 edition, said the state authority's consultant, Price Waterhouse, raised red flags about the deal.

The paper added Lockheed was a corporate descendant of Lockheed Information Management Services, a data processing giant that was involved in contracting scandals under former mayors David Dinkins and Ed Koch.

The Giuliani Administration in April, 1994, announced that the city and Lockheed Information Management Services had agreed it would not do business with the city for four years. In return, New York City agreed not to begin a debarment proceeding against the firm based on an August 1993 report from the New York City Department of Investigation.

A summary of the 201-page report, which Mayor Dinkins requested, focused on how Lockheed Information Management Services was recommended for a $150 million contract. The document, provided by Giuliani's office, found the budget director had shown favoritism toward the company while New York City was considering the firm's proposal to privatize parking management services.
A spokesman for Lockheed was not immediately available to comment.
The report found Lockheed Information Management Services had "employment discussions" with the chief of staff of the city's first deputy mayor, violating company policy.
The firm denied it had commited any act that warranted debarment and was prepared to defend itself against such charges, the summary report said.
